summary:
Silent Monuments is an interactive web project that introduces school-age children to the stories of spacecraft left on the Moon and Mars. In a three-dimensional exploration environment, users can select spacecraft and listen to or read stories told from the vehicles’ perspectives. Covering nine story groups, the experience combines NASA-sourced mission information with learning questions, collectible cards, and historical newspaper-style storytelling.

Our project transforms technical information about past space missions into stories children can understand. It explains why each spacecraft was sent, what instruments it used, and how it contributed to science. We distinguish creative storytelling from factual mission information to support scientific accuracy.

The discoveries made by these spacecraft remain valuable long after their missions end. Through Silent Monuments, we aim to bring this scientific heritage to life, spark children’s interest in space, and encourage them to ask their own questions about exploration.
details:
Silent Monuments is an interactive educational web experience that introduces school-age children to spacecraft and scientific equipment left on the Moon and Mars. It explores why these machines were sent, how they worked, and what their discoveries taught us.

Users begin by selecting the Moon or Mars in a three-dimensional environment. They can then explore equipment markers, listen to stories narrated from the spacecraft’s perspective, or read the accompanying text. The project includes nine story groups covering Apollo hardware and robotic explorers. Collectible cards and questions encourage participation, while a timeline and historical newspaper-style features connect space exploration with events on Earth.

Each story includes a learning section that explains the relationship between an instrument, its task, and its scientific contribution. For example, InSight’s seismometer recorded ground vibrations that helped scientists investigate the interior of Mars. Short questions provide feedback and encourage users to revisit the explanations.

We built the project using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Three.js for the 3D scenes and the Web Audio API for interactive sound effects. Recorded narration supports the storytelling. The current content is in Turkish, and users can access both audio and written versions of the stories.

Our creative approach gives spacecraft a voice while keeping fictional storytelling separate from mission facts. NASA-linked information panels provide mission dates, locations, and status details. Vehicles featured together, such as Spirit and Opportunity, have separate records to avoid confusing their histories. We also clarify that in-game restoration represents bringing a story to life, rather than repairing a real spacecraft.

During development, we focused on balancing engaging storytelling with scientific accuracy, keeping explanations understandable, and connecting game activities to learning. Our intended impact is to make the scientific legacy of past missions more approachable and inspire children to ask questions about space and engineering.

The next steps are to test the experience with children, evaluate what they understand, and improve keyboard and screen-reader accessibility. Its educational impact has not yet been measured through user testing.
